stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu makes landfall, Andhra on alert as storm unleashes 120 kmph winds
stories.title: Cyclone Murasu makes landfall, Andhra on alert as storm unleashes 120 kmph winds
stories.summary: Cyclone Murasu makes landfall, Andhra on alert as storm unleashes 120 kmph winds
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Cyclone Murasu began making landfall near Ongole with heavy rain and gale-force winds.
The storm prompted flight cancellations, surge warnings and large-scale restoration preparations.

Severe cyclonic storm Murasu began its landfall process near Ongole in Andhra Pradesh's Prakasam district around 1 am on Tuesday, bringing heavy rainfall and gale-force winds of up to 110 kmph, with gusts reaching 120 kmph, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said.
In its bulletin at 1.30 am, the IMD said the cyclone was centred over the west-central Bay of Bengal, around 40 km southeast of Ongole, 60 km northeast of Kavali and 70 km south of Bapatla.
The forward sector of the cyclone's wall cloud had started entering the coast, with the landfall process expected to continue through the early hours.
The IMD warned that gale-force winds of 110 kmph, gusting up to 120 kmph, were likely along and off the South Andhra Pradesh coast until morning.
Heavy rainfall was also forecast across South Coastal Andhra Pradesh over the next 12 hours.
A storm surge of 1-1.5 metres above the astronomical tide was likely to inundate low-lying areas until Wednesday morning.
Bapatla, Krishna and Prakasam districts were expected to witness the maximum impact of the surge.
At least 19 domestic flights across Vijayawada, Tirupati and Visakhapatnam airports were cancelled on Monday as the cyclone approached the Andhra Pradesh coast.
Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu has directed officials to remain on high alert and take all necessary precautionary measures to prevent loss of life and property.

During a review meeting on Monday, Naidu said the impact of Murasu was likely to be less severe than Cyclone Arnab but stressed the need for effective preparedness as moderate to heavy rainfall was expected across South Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema districts.

stories.headline: Maharashtra sets up drought mitigation panel, approves ₹291.91 crore relief for flood-hit farmers
stories.title: Maharashtra sets up drought mitigation panel, approves ₹291.91 crore relief for flood-hit farmers
stories.summary: The measures follow deficient rainfall in parts of Maharashtra during 2026, prompting the government to declare drought in talukas identified under the Kharif season’s Trigger-1 assessment
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Maharashtra government on Monday (November 1, 2026) announced measures to address drought and flood-related agricultural distress across the State, constituting a high-level committee headed by the Chief Minister to oversee soil and water conservation projects in drought-affected areas and approving ₹291.91 crore in financial assistance for farmers affected by heavy rainfall and flooding between June and August 2026.

Soil and Water Conservation Minister Sanjay Rathod said the committee would monitor conservation projects undertaken through non-governmental organisations, including Paani Foundation and Chandra Foundation, as part of the state’s drought mitigation efforts.
The government has also decided to revive Paani Foundation’s Water Cup competition to encourage community participation in water conservation.
The measures follow deficient rainfall in parts of Maharashtra during 2026, prompting the government to declare drought in talukas identified under the Kharif season’s Trigger-1 assessment.

According to a government resolution issued on November 2, all Deputy Chief Ministers will serve as co-chairpersons of the high-level committee, which will include ministers from departments such as agriculture, water resources, rural development and employment guarantee.
A separate executive committee, chaired by the Principal Secretary of the Water Resources Department, will coordinate implementation and meet at least once a month.
Progress will be monitored using geographical information systems (GIS), satellite imagery, mobile-based monitoring systems and online dashboards.

Meanwhile, Relief and Rehabilitation Minister Makarand Jadhav Patil announced that the government had sanctioned ₹262.70 crore for crop damage affecting 3,09,289 farmers across six revenue divisions, including Pune, Nagpur, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Amravati, Konkan and Nashik.
An additional ₹29.21 crore has been approved for damage to agricultural land covering 7,675.40 hectares belonging to 34,984 farmers.
The assistance will cover eligible restoration work, including the removal of sand, silt and salt deposits caused by flooding.

Crop damage compensation will be transferred directly to eligible farmers’ bank accounts, while small and marginal landowners will receive assistance for damaged agricultural land up to a maximum of two hectares, in accordance with prescribed norms.
The government has also directed district collectors to ensure that banks do not divert disaster relief payments towards loan repayments or other recoveries.

stories.headline: Russia’s increased attacks on Ukraine’s energy, heating infrastructure ‘creating a deadly situation for civilians’, Amnesty International warns
stories.title: Russia’s increased attacks on Ukraine’s energy, heating infrastructure ‘creating a deadly situation for civilians’, Amnesty International warns
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 2: Russia’s increased targeted attacks on Ukraine’s energy and heating infrastructure risks creating a new humanitarian catastrophe for civilians ahead of winter, Amnesty International warned today. It said the civilian death toll during Russia’s full-scale ‘illegal’ invasion has increased significantly in recent months, with October 2026 expected to be one of the deadliest periods for civilians in years. Based on prior Russian military attacks in the approach to previous winters, there is overwhelming evidence that the deliberate targeting of energy and heating infrastructure intended to cause civilian suffering will result in immense harm. The International Criminal Court (ICC) has indicted Russia’s Lieutenant General Sergei Ivanovich Kobylash and Admiral Viktor Nikolayevich Sokolov on charges of war crimes for allegedly directing attacks on Ukrainian electrical infrastructure. “The Russian Federation is once again implementing a large-scale campaign against Ukrainian energy and heating infrastructure ahead of a freezing winter, including attacks far from the front lines of conflict,” said Scott Edwards, Director of Amnesty International’s Crisis Response Programme. “These attacks on essential infrastructure are creating a deadly situation for civilians, who directly suffer the consequences. This is an illegal campaign, carried out with flagrant disregard for the rules of war, and appears to be designed to create unliveable conditions for Ukrainian civilians. “Whatever the motives behind the Kremlin’s plan to make life unbearable for civilians, it is criminal and cannot be tolerated. World leaders seeking to end this conflict must immediately use their leverage to minimize any potential harm to civilians, before another intentional humanitarian catastrophe begins with the arrival of winter.” On 26 October, the International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine reported that Russia had committed war crimes and crimes against humanity in Ukraine by intentionally attacking energy infrastructure, leaving millions of people without electricity and heat in freezing temperatures. Amnesty International has previously documented how Russia’s widespread attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure may constitute war crimes and highlighted their life-threatening consequences for the civilian population. Civilian casualties and widespread power cuts The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine found that at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured in September 2026 as a result of Russian attacks, an 85% increase over September 2025. Casualties were recorded in 22 of 24 regions in Ukraine. The Mission also described the first half of October 2026 as one of the deadliest periods for civilians in years. On 13 and 14 October, strikes reportedly hit multiple energy installations, including Kyiv’s three principal power stations, temporarily leaving approximately 600,000 people without electricity. On 17 October, further Russian attacks reportedly killed at least eight people, injured 60 and interrupted electricity supplies to more than one million people across nine regions. Both the Russian Ministry of Defence and President Vladimir Putin have made public statements announcing intentional attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Prior attacks on energy and heating infrastructure in Ukraine caused widespread and widely reported civilian suffering that is known to Russian military and strategic planners. During the winter of 2025–2026, the Russian Armed Forces carried out at least 423 attacks on electricity infrastructure and 74 strikes on heating facilities, according to UN monitoring. These attacks caused rolling outages affecting millions of people and interrupted heating for hundreds of thousands as temperatures fell below -20°C. The resulting loss of electricity, water and heating disrupted healthcare and education, and also disproportionately harmed older people, persons with disabilities, women and families with children. Under international humanitarian law, electricity and heating installations are civilian objects unless and for such time as they meet the strict definition of a military objective. Even where an installation constitutes a military objective, attacking forces must comply with the principles of distinction, proportionality and precaution. Intentionally directing attacks against civilian objects, launching indiscriminate attacks, or carrying out attacks expected to cause excessive civilian harm in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated can constitute war crimes. Ensuring accountability for such crimes requires strong and independent international justice mechanisms capable of investigating and prosecuting those responsible, including the most senior officials. Meanwhile, the US administration is currently engaged in a campaign to dismantle the work of the ICC. Amnesty International has called for all relevant states to take appropriate measures to resist this attack and actively protect the Court and the broader international justice system. President Vladimir Putin is wanted on charges of war crimes by the ICC, and Amnesty International has called for President Putin to be arrested and surrendered to the ICC by any parties in a position to do so. Calls to Russian authorities Amnesty International called on Russian forces to end their systematic attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The Russian authorities must also immediately end other violations of international humanitarian law, including attacks on other civilian infrastructure in Ukraine, such as residential buildings, hospitals, and schools, and end its campaign of targeting non-combatants. All parties to the conflict must respect the principles of distinction, proportionality and precaution and protect civilians and civilian objects. States supporting accountability mechanisms must provide the expertise and resources needed to effectively investigate allegations of violations, secure evidence, and identify suspected perpetrators, including commanders and senior officials who may bear responsibility. All states must urgently act to protect the functioning of the ICC and should execute arrest warrants when and where they can.
